evidence: Single package 'CYNITE' with all core application logic, plus a 'database' package — indicating clear modular separation within one deployable unit
No external service communication (e.g., no REST/gRPC clients, message queues), no service discovery, no orchestration — rules out microservices
Heavy interdependencies between modules (e.g., CYNITE/* modules import from database/*, utils, info) — typical of monoliths with modules, not layered/hexagonal
Main entry point is a single 'bot.py' instantiating a Pyrogram Client — centralized startup, not distributed
Use of shared utilities (utils.py) and global config (info.py) across all modules — characteristic of modular monoliths in Python bots

No clear separation of core domain vs infrastructure interfaces (e.g., no adapters/ports abstraction), and no strict dependency direction (all layers depend on each other) — rules out layered/hexagonal/MVC
Files like Script.py, utils.py, info.py contain loose utilities — script-like composition, but organized in packages suggests intentional modularity
risks: High coupling due to circular imports and shared mutable state (e.g., 'temp' object in utils.py used across modules)
Testing difficulty: modules depend heavily on global state and external services (Pyrogram, MongoDB)
Scalability limitations: monolithic deployment prevents independent scaling of features
Maintainability risk: 'mi_avg': 0 indicates poor maintainability metrics; modules are not truly decoupled despite directory separation
